tagline: Granite battle markers and Chickasaw history along rural Mississippi roads
intro: The Brice’s Crossroads Battlefield-Chief Tishomingo route links Baldwyn and Guntown through country that is largely rural and agricultural. Granite markers along Highway 370 explain the battle fought here on June 10, 1864. The corridor management plan makes its case for scenic-byway designation through Civil War, Native American and early African American histories in a rural landscape.

The driving route grew from battlefield preservation and interpretation. A state grant, artifacts donated by the Claude Gentry family and land donated by the Haynes family helped establish the interpretive center, which opened in 1998. Identification of Chief Tishomingo’s home site led organizers to extend the proposed byway to include it and other Chickasaw historical sites. Chickasaw Governor Bill Anoatubby supported the designation effort. The corridor also includes Chickasaw home sites on Reynoldsburg Road, which the Chickasaws built partly with U.S. government funds as an alternative to the Natchez Trace into middle Tennessee.

The planned journey begins at the interpretive center on Grisham Street in Baldwyn and follows MS 370 toward the battlefield. The national battlefield site lies west of Baldwyn on Highway 370. County Roads 833 and 503 then lead to MS 348 at Blair, with the route ending at MS 145 in Guntown.

moments.title: Brices Cross Roads National Battlefield Site
moments.text: A one-acre grassy park marks the place where the Brice family house stood. It contains a flagpole, a memorial monument and two cannons. Here, on June 10, 1864, Nathan Bedford Forrest’s smaller Confederate force defeated a U.S. Army force. The neighboring Old Bethany Cemetery contains the graves of more than 90 Confederate soldiers killed in the battle. U.S. Army dead were first buried in common graves on the battlefield and later reinterred in Memphis National Cemetery. The modern Bethany church occupies a different site from the congregation’s wartime meeting house.

moments.title: Tishomingo Creek
moments.text: The wartime bridge over Tishomingo Creek became a bottleneck during the Union retreat. Abandoned wagons and dead pack animals blocked the crossing, and many Federal soldiers tried to swim or ford the creek under Confederate fire. At the nearby overlook, Forrest directed Confederate cannon forward to fire without infantry support during the battle. A later pedestrian bridge was built at the location of that crossing. The creek bears Chief Tishomingo’s name, and the Chickasaw Nation honors him with his image at the center of its national seal.

moments.title: Guntown
moments.text: Guntown’s older streets lie east of Highway 145 near the railroad tracks. During the Civil War, United States Cavalry officers described it as a station and small village on the Mobile & Ohio railroad. The town was incorporated in 1867. Its name reaches further back, to Virginia loyalist James G. Gunn, who found asylum among the Chickasaw in what is now Lee County.
